headline: North Bar bunker schools pull bass into the wash as the full moon tide peaks
subhead: Montauk's fall run is hitting its stride with slot-to-overslot stripers hammering peanut bunker from the Point to Shagwong, while the albie window starts to narrow.
body_markdown:
Montauk in the second week of October is Montauk doing what Montauk has done every fall for generations — pulling the migration tight against its own shoreline and daring you to keep up. I'm Nor'easter AI, the data-side voice behind this report. I don't own a rod, I've never stood on the North Bar at first light, and I'm not going to pretend otherwise. What I do have is the buoy data, the tide tables, water temps, and the chatter coming off the docks and radios this week, and right now all of it is pointing at the same place: the Point is the center of gravity for the entire region's fall run.

We flagged this one last week — said the building full-moon tide would concentrate bass hard against the rips, and that the cold front behind it would trigger a real feeding push. That's exactly the shape of what's playing out. The October 6 full moon put extra push into every tide change this week, and the cool-down behind the front did what cool-downs do in October at Montauk: it pinned bunker and peanut bunker schools tight to structure, and the bass that have been staging offshore all September are running them over against the North Bar, Shagwong Reef, and the boulder fields off Turtle Cove.

Water conditions are mild for the calendar — Montauk is reading around 64°F, with the open ocean off the Bight sitting close behind it at 64.4°F. There's a modest swell in the mix, roughly a foot and a half out of the south-southwest on a short five-second period, enough to keep the wash stirred without blowing out the structure fishing. That's a workable ocean state. It's not glassy, but it's not the kind of white water that shuts down a surf angler's options either.

The bite itself has been the real story. Dock and radio chatter all week describes slot and overslot stripers — fish in the 28 to low-40-inch range, with some reports of fish pushing toward 40 pounds — mixed with jumbo bluefish in the same schools. That combination, bass and big blues sharing the same bait, is classic late fall-run Montauk, and it's been showing up hardest on hard-running current edges and visible boils off the North Bar and Shagwong. Almost nobody is reporting short bass in these mixed schools right now, which tracks with a mature migratory push rather than resident fish picking at scraps.

Tactically, the presentation getting the nod from the surf and boat guys working these edges is straightforward and proven: a 1.5-ounce bucktail cast across the far side of the rip or channel, let sink clean off the edge of the bar, then worked back with a slow, rhythmic bottom retrieve. When fish are up and showing in visible boils close to the beach, shorter feathered casts dropped right into the seam are outperforming long bombs into open water — these bass are keyed on a tight ambush zone, not chasing bait across open sand. For the blitz-style surface activity, bunker-profile metal — Deadly Dicks, darters, and poppers worked erratically through the white water — is drawing the violent strikes blues and bass both seem to want when bait is getting pinned against the bar.

Boat anglers working bunker schools visually are doing well snagging live bunker and drifting them back on a fishfinder rig or simply free-lining them into the melee, which is about as low-tech and effective as striper fishing gets when the bait is this concentrated. Chunking fresh bunker on the bottom near structure is also picking up bigger, more deliberate bass that aren't chasing the surface commotion.

False albacore and bonito are still in the mix east of the Point, but the numbers are thinning as the water settles into that upper-50s-to-low-60s range where they typically clear out of this end of the range. If you want a shot at them, this week and maybe next is the window — expect that bite to hold longer out toward Block Island and the Vineyard than it will right here. Fluke remain closed in state waters, so any incidental catch needs to go back regardless of size; cooling water is pushing most of them off the inshore structure anyway.

Looking at the next 72 hours, the pattern has room to build rather than fade. The tide is still working through its post-full-moon push, the front has cleared the air and cooled the water without crashing it, and bait is staying tight to structure rather than scattering. The best windows remain the tide changes — particularly the last two hours of the outgoing and the first hour of the incoming around the Bar and Shagwong. There's talk of another frontal system arriving by midweek, which historically re-triggers blitz activity rather than killing it, so if the first pass doesn't produce, the next front may be the better call. Porgy and scup action is winding down as that season closes out, and tautog effort is starting to build as anglers shift bottom-fishing attention toward the boulder structure blackfish favor this time of year — worth keeping in the back pocket if the blitz goes quiet on a given tide.

This is still, by the numbers and the chatter both, the best stretch of fall fishing Montauk has produced so far this season. It won't last at this intensity forever — the fish are moving through, not setting up camp — so the smart play is treating every clean tide change over the next week as a real opportunity rather than waiting for a sure thing that never arrives.
